properties.natural_language: The custody group requirement must be clamped between VALIDATOR_CUSTODY_REQUIREMENT (8) and NUMBER_OF_CUSTODY_GROUPS, regardless of the validator's effective balance.
The validator effective balance must be known and non-negative before computing custody group requirements.
After custody groups are determined, the node must advertise its custody count in ENR metadata and begin downloading columns for all assigned custody groups.
The computed custody group count must always satisfy: VALIDATOR_CUSTODY_REQUIREMENT <= custody_count <= NUMBER_OF_CUSTODY_GROUPS.
Custody adjustments must occur at epoch boundaries when effective balance is recalculated, not mid-epoch.
The highest custody requirement must persist across restarts until explicitly recalculated based on the current validator set.
The network must have sufficient total custody coverage across all nodes so that every column is custodied by multiple peers.
Validators must have sufficient storage and bandwidth to custody their required number of groups (minimum 8) per slot.
The execution engine must provide cell-based proofs via engine_getPayloadV5 that are consistent with the blob commitments before column sidecar construction can proceed.
After column sidecar construction, each sidecar must represent a complete vertical slice across all blobs, and all sidecars must be ready for distribution.
After publishing to subnet topics, each sidecar must be distributed to its correct data_column_sidecar_{subnet_id} pubsub topic.
A column sidecar must be within the retention window (age < MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_DATA_COLUMN_SIDECARS_REQUESTS) to be required for serving to peers.
After a sidecar exceeds MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_DATA_COLUMN_SIDECARS_REQUESTS, it may be pruned and the node has no obligation to serve it.
A sidecar within the retention window must always be retained and available for serving to requesting peers; it must not be pruned.
Contract bytecode must be fully loaded before valid jump destination analysis can begin.

After valid jump destination analysis, the computed set must contain only positions that (a) are within bytecode bounds, (b) contain the JUMPDEST opcode (0x5B), and (c) are not within PUSH instruction data segments.
The set of valid jump destinations for a given contract bytecode must remain constant throughout the execution of that contract call.
No jump destination within a PUSH instruction data segment can ever be in the valid set, preventing execution of arbitrary byte sequences as opcodes.
Contract bytecode is immutable after deployment, so valid jump destinations cannot change between calls.
Invalid opcodes during bytecode iteration must be treated as single-byte instructions, not causing analysis failure.
PUSH instructions at the end of bytecode that would reference out-of-bounds data must still be valid but push zero-padded values during execution.
After executing JUMP/JUMPI, if the destination is not in the valid jump set, execution must halt with an exception and all remaining gas consumed.
After a valid jump, the program counter must be updated to the exact validated destination address and execution must continue from that point.
The EVM program counter can only be set to addresses that are in the pre-computed valid jump destination set during JUMP/JUMPI execution.
After PUSH instruction analysis, all bytes in PUSH data segments must be marked as invalid jump destinations.
During bytecode iteration, the data size for PUSH-N instructions must always equal (opcode - 0x5F) bytes, covering PUSH1 (1 byte) through PUSH32 (32 bytes).
Every byte position in the bytecode must be classified as either an opcode position or a PUSH data position, with no ambiguity.
After on_block processing, the block must be recorded with PENDING payload status in the fork choice store, awaiting execution payload verification.
After on_execution_payload completes with valid payload and data availability, the block's payload status must transition from PENDING to FULL.
A block's payload status can only transition from PENDING to either FULL or EMPTY, never backwards from FULL to PENDING or EMPTY to PENDING.
When constructing parent state in on_block, execution_payload_states (FULL) must take priority over block_states (EMPTY) when both exist for the same parent block hash.
PTC payload timeliness requires both: more than 256 affirmative votes out of 512 PTC members AND the payload must exist in execution_payload_states.
After on_payload_attestation_message processing, the ptc_vote boolean vector must be updated at the correct validator index within the assigned committee.
An attacker must not be able to control a majority of PTC committee validators (>256 of 512) for a given slot.
PTC committee members must honestly report payload presence based on their actual observation; colluding majority could manipulate fork choice between FULL and EMPTY tracks.
Proposer boost can only be applied if: (a) parent block is from a non-previous slot, OR (b) parent from previous slot has sufficient weight threshold AND no early equivocations from the proposer.
If an equivocation is detected from the proposer, proposer boost must be denied for that block.
The weight threshold for proposer boost conditions must follow the established proposer boost percentage from the base fork choice specification.
Early equivocations are defined as equivocations detected before the attestation deadline within the slot.
The execution payload envelope must arrive within the PTC deadline for honest proposers to avoid unfair penalization to EMPTY status.
EIP-4844 must be active and blob gas price must be available in the block header before BLOBBASEFEE opcode can be executed.
After BLOBBASEFEE execution, the blob base fee value must be pushed as a left-padded 32-byte value onto the EVM stack.
After BLOBBASEFEE execution, exactly 2 gas units must be deducted from remaining execution gas.
The gas cost of BLOBBASEFEE is fixed at exactly 2 gas, matching the BASEFEE opcode cost, with no variability.
At least 2 gas must remain before BLOBBASEFEE execution; otherwise, the operation must revert with out-of-gas.
The blob base fee value returned by BLOBBASEFEE must accurately reflect the actual blob gas market conditions as computed by get_blob_gasprice(header).
BLOBBASEFEE must be treated as an invalid opcode on chains or blocks without EIP-4844 enabled, causing execution to revert.
After a rollup contract executes BLOBBASEFEE, the returned value must provide trustless access to the current blob base fee without relying on external oracles.
Before any push operation, the stack size must be checked against the 1024 element maximum; push must be rejected if stack is full.
Before any pop operation, the stack must be checked for non-emptiness; pop must be rejected if stack has 0 elements.
After a successful push, the stack size must increase by exactly 1 and the pushed value must be at the top of the stack.
After a successful pop, the stack size must decrease by exactly 1 and the returned value must be the element that was at the top.
After StackOverflowError, execution must halt immediately with all gas consumed.
After StackUnderflowError, execution must halt immediately with all gas consumed.
The EVM stack size must always be between 0 and 1024 elements inclusive at any point during execution.
All U256 values stored on the stack must be retrievable without loss or truncation.
No combination of opcodes can bypass stack bounds checks to corrupt the stack state.
Before opcode execution, the stack must be validated to have enough input elements and sufficient space for output elements.
Contract deployment bytecode returned from init code execution must be compared against MAX_CODE_SIZE (24576 bytes) before storage.
If returned bytecode is <= 24576 bytes, the contract must be deployed and stored at the contract address in the state trie.
If returned bytecode exceeds 24576 bytes, contract creation must fail with out-of-gas exception consuming all remaining gas, and no contract is deployed.
No contract on the Ethereum state can have code size exceeding 24576 bytes (post-EIP-170 activation).
The MAX_CODE_SIZE limit (24576 bytes) must be applied consistently across all client implementations to maintain consensus.
The code size limit applies only to the returned deployment bytecode, not to the init code itself.
Contracts of exactly 24576 bytes are valid; only contracts with length > 24576 trigger failure (strict inequality).
When contract creation fails due to size limit violation, all remaining gas is consumed with no refund issued.
The size limit bounds the maximum verification work per block for contract creations, preventing DoS attacks against light clients.
After Petersburg activation, EIP-1283 net gas metering for SSTORE must be disabled and SSTORE operations must use pre-Constantinople gas metering rules.
When Petersburg and Constantinople activate at the same block, the net effect must be Constantinople features minus EIP-1283.
Petersburg takes precedence over Constantinople when both activate at the same block, effectively overriding EIP-1283 inclusion.
All client implementations must correctly implement the fork precedence logic to maintain consensus.
After reverting SSTORE pricing, the reentrancy attack vector enabled by cheap SSTORE operations must be eliminated.
Node operators must upgrade to Petersburg-aware clients before block 7,280,000 to avoid forking off on a separate chain.
The eth_txGasLimitCap RPC request must use empty params and the node must compute min(protocolCap, policyCap) as the effective limit.
After computing the effective cap, the node must return a QUANTITY hex value if a finite cap exists, or null if no finite cap exists.
The effective gas cap must always be min(protocolCap, policyCap) when both exist; protocolCap alone when no policy cap; policyCap alone when no protocol cap; null when neither exists.
PolicyCap is only for mempool admission policy, not consensus; transactions above policyCap but below protocolCap can still be included by other nodes.
After a wallet queries gas cap and estimates transaction gas, if the estimated gas exceeds the cap, the user must be warned before submission.
The node must be trusted to return accurate cap information; a malicious node could return incorrect caps causing transaction failures.
Clients should re-query the gas cap after known hard forks, as the protocol cap may change at fork boundaries.
After the changes freeze, no more EIP additions are permitted to the hard fork Meta EIP.
After the hard fork activates on the network, the Meta EIP must be finalized and immutable.
The Meta EIP state must transition strictly forward: Draft -> Accepted -> Final, with no backwards transitions.
An EIP proposed for inclusion must have implementations from major clients and pass security review before acceptance.
If an EIP has known security issues, it must be rejected from the hard fork.
If an EIP's implementation deadline passes without major client implementations, the EIP must be rejected from the hard fork.
The hard fork timeline must follow the sequential order: acceptance deadline -> implementation deadline -> testnet date -> mainnet activation block.
The All Core Devs group must act in good faith for the governance process to produce secure hard fork specifications.
The majority of the network must upgrade before the activation block to prevent chain splits.
The eth_getProof request must include a valid address, list of storage keys, and block identifier.
After proof generation, the accountProof must contain all RLP-serialized Merkle-Patricia trie nodes from stateRoot to the target account.
For each requested storage key, the storageProof must contain all trie nodes from storageHash to the key-value pair.
An attacker cannot forge Merkle proofs that validate against the correct stateRoot, ensuring state spoofing is impossible.
The verifier must have access to a trusted block header with stateRoot from a reliable source (beacon chain, light client) before proof verification.
After cryptographic verification against trusted stateRoot, data from an untrusted RPC provider becomes trustworthy.
If any hash in the proof chain does not match, the proof must be marked invalid and data cannot be trusted.
Non-existence of an account or storage value must be provable by following the path until divergence or empty branch.
The RPC endpoint must have access to the full state trie for the requested block; pruned state must result in an error response.
Implementation-defined limits on the number of storage keys must exist to prevent DoS attacks against the RPC endpoint.
